• Standard error of the difference = sqrt(p1 (1 - p1) / n1 + p2 (1 - p2) / n2) = sqrt(0.1 x 0.9 / 10000 + 0.108 x 0.892 / 10000) ≈ sqrt(0.000009 + 0.00000963) ≈ 0.00432.
• z = 0.008 / 0.00432 ≈ 1.85, below 1.96, so not significant at 5% two-sided (p ≈ 0.064).
• 95% interval: 0.008 ± 1.96 x 0.00432 ≈ (-0.05, +1.65) percentage points. It includes zero.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What do you tell the product manager? The data are consistent with anything from no effect to a 1.6-point lift. If a lift of this size would matter, the test was underpowered: about 16 x 0.1 x 0.9 / 0.008^2 ≈ 22,500 users per arm are needed for 80% power, so run it longer.

cards.title: Causal inference without an experiment
cards.question: You cannot run an A/B test. Name the main ways to estimate a causal effect from observational data and what each assumes.
cards.answer:
• Difference-in-differences: compare the change over time in a treated group with the change in an untreated group. Assumes the two would have moved in parallel without the treatment.
• Propensity methods (matching, inverse propensity weighting): model the probability of treatment given covariates and balance the groups on it. Assumes no unmeasured confounders and that every kind of unit had some chance of either treatment.
• Instrumental variables: use something that changes treatment but affects the outcome only through it (for example a randomised nudge). Assumes that exclusion holds; estimates the effect for those the instrument moves.
• Regression discontinuity: compare units just either side of a threshold that assigns treatment. Assumes nothing else changes at the threshold; estimates a local effect.
• Synthetic control: build a weighted mix of untreated units that tracked the treated unit before the change.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Which assumption can you test? Parallel trends and balance can be checked on pre-treatment data; no unmeasured confounding cannot be. Say so, and run a placebo or sensitivity analysis. Netflix publishes heavily on causal inference, so expect this where an A/B test is impractical.

cards.title: Off-policy estimators
cards.question: Compare the direct method, inverse propensity scoring, self-normalised IPS and doubly robust estimation for evaluating a new recommendation policy on logged data.
cards.answer:
• Direct method: fit a reward model and average its predictions under the new policy. Low variance, biased wherever the reward model is wrong.
• IPS: average of reward x (new policy probability / logging probability) over logged actions. Unbiased if propensities are correct and the logging policy gave every action the new one can take some probability; variance explodes when weights are large.
• Self-normalised IPS: divide by the sum of the weights instead of n. Slightly biased, much lower variance. Clipping weights makes the same trade.
• Doubly robust: direct-method estimate plus an IPS-weighted correction of its residuals. Consistent if either the reward model or the propensities are right, and usually lower variance than IPS.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Why do these struggle for ranked lists? The action is a whole slate, so the exact logged slate has a tiny propensity. Practical answers are slate estimators with position-level assumptions, small action spaces, or interleaving and A/B tests for the final call.

cards.title: Model choice
cards.question: Tell me about a model you shipped. Why that model and not a simpler one?
cards.answer:
• Name the baseline (a heuristic or a linear model) and its number on the metric that mattered.
• Give the lift of the shipped model over it, offline and online.
• Say what the complexity cost: latency, serving cost, on-call burden, iteration speed.
• Name one alternative you rejected and the evidence that decided it.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Would you make the same choice today? A staff-level answer changes something and says what you learned.

cards.title: Labels
cards.question: What was the label for that model, where did it come from, and how could it be wrong?
cards.answer:
• Define the label exactly, including the time window.
• Say who or what produced it (user action, human rater, downstream system) and how delayed it was.
• Name its biases: selection by the previous model, position, missing negatives, rater disagreement.
• Say what you did about one of them and how you measured the effect.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How did you know the label tracked what the business cared about? Name the validation: a correlation study, a holdout, a survey.

cards.title: Offline versus online
cards.question: Describe a time offline metrics and the A/B test disagreed.
cards.answer:
• State both results with numbers.
• Give your hypotheses in the order you tested them (skew, selection bias, metric mismatch, novelty).
• Say what the evidence showed and what you changed in the evaluation afterwards.
• Say what you shipped, or did not, and why.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What do you now check before trusting an offline win?

cards.title: Failure in production
cards.question: Tell me about a model or pipeline of yours that failed in production.
cards.answer:
• What users or the business saw, and for how long.
• How it was detected: an alert you had built, or a person noticing.
• Root cause, in one sentence a non-specialist could follow.
• The immediate fix, then what you changed so that class of failure cannot recur.
• Your own part in the cause, stated plainly.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What would have caught it a day earlier?

cards.title: Scope and influence
cards.question: Describe a technical decision you drove across teams where people disagreed.
cards.answer:
• The decision and why it mattered beyond your team.
• The strongest version of the other side's position.
• What you did to resolve it: data, a prototype, a written proposal, a timeboxed experiment.
• The outcome, including what you conceded.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Which part of the result was yours and which was the team's? Be exact; interviewers probe for inflated ownership.

cards.title: Trade-offs under constraint
cards.question: What would you have done differently with half the time? With twice the time?
cards.answer:
• Half: what you would cut first and the risk that accepts.
• Twice: the one investment with the highest expected return, and why not the others.
• Show that the original plan was a choice among options, not the only path.
cards.key_concept: Probe — What did you deliberately not build, and has that decision held up?

cards.title: Why this company (Anthropic)
cards.question: Why do you want to work on AI at a company focused on safety, and what worries you about it?
cards.answer:
• A specific reason tied to your own work or reading, not a summary of the website.
• A view on at least one real risk or trade-off, held with reasons and stated with its uncertainty.
• Evidence you have read primary material: the company's published research or policies. Read them before the interview.
• How the role you are applying for connects to that.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Where do you disagree with the company's approach? Having no disagreement reads as not having thought about it.

cards.title: Feedback and candour (Netflix)
cards.question: Tell me about hard feedback you gave a peer or a manager, and hard feedback you received.
cards.answer:
• The situation and why the feedback was needed.
• What you said, close to the actual words, and how you delivered it.
• What happened afterwards.
• For feedback received: what you changed, with a concrete before and after.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Netflix publishes a culture memo and interviews against it. Read the current version on its jobs site and prepare one story for each behaviour it names. This card does not quote it: the site was not reachable when the card was written.

cards.title: Judgment without process
cards.question: Describe a decision you made without asking permission that carried real risk.
cards.answer:
• The context you had and how you got it.
• Why you judged it yours to make, and who you informed.
• The outcome, good or bad.
• What you would do the same and differently.
cards.key_concept: Probe — How do you decide when to act and when to ask? Give your actual rule.

cards.title: Depth check
cards.question: Pick the most technically difficult part of your last project and teach it to me.
cards.answer:
• Start from the problem, not the solution.
• One level of detail deeper than feels necessary: the equation, the data structure, the failure case.
• What you tried that did not work.
• What you still do not understand about it.
cards.key_concept: Probe — Interviewers keep asking "why" until you reach the edge of what you know. Saying "I don't know, here is how I would find out" at that edge is the right answer.
